evidence.locator: line 53 SHA-256 ee7617e3af48cbe20347dba3c1c4d2a268848fe98f4173ca58582115a020159f; primary text: Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan (1651), Part I, chapter XIII 'Of the Natural Condition of Mankind as concerning their Felicity and Misery' (Project Gutenberg ebook 3207; Fordham Internet History Sourcebook 'Thomas Hobbes: Leviathan, Chaps 13-14, 1651', sourcebooks.web.fordham.edu/mod/hobbes-lev13.asp), consulted 2026-11-07 through web copies of the chapter, not a page-cited printed edition
evidence.explanation: SOURCE WORDING (kept exactly as printed, not corrected): 'Thomas Hobbes referred to as a primitive society. This is a society where life is solitary, poor, wicked and short.' PRIMARY WORDING, recorded here only as verification evidence: the chapter describes the life of man in that condition as 'solitary, poore, nasty, brutish, and short' (1651 spelling; modern 'poor'). Findings: (a) 'wicked' is not Hobbes's word and 'nasty, brutish' are missing from the source's version, so the source line is not a faithful quotation of Hobbes; (b) 'primitive society' is not Hobbes's term: his chapter is about the natural condition of mankind, a condition with no common power to keep all in awe, which he describes as a war of every man against every man, so teaching it as Hobbes's 'theory of a primitive society' misdescribes the argument; (c) in the same chapter Hobbes illustrates with peoples of America, a seventeenth-century illustration that a lesson must attribute to Hobbes and not state as established fact about any people.

open_items.detail: The ten-function list at getBody lines 124–135 mixes constitutional powers, policy objectives and broad textbook descriptions. Section 17(3)(a) describes opportunities for suitable employment, not a promise that government directly provides every job. The prison claim needs a correctional-law check.
open_items.required_action: In GOV-LES-T1-W02-CORRECTED-WEEK, retain the list as an attributed textbook classification, distinguish powers under ss.4–6 from policy objectives under ss.14–19, qualify employment as an opportunity/policy objective, and verify the prison/correctional-service point against applicable law. open_items.detail: Week Two line 144 states: 'The ultimate aim of government is to make us political scientists'. This confuses the educational value of studying Government with the purpose of government. Constitution s.14(2)(b) identifies security and welfare as government's primary purpose; OpenStax describes political science as the systematic study of political phenomena and notes there is no unanimity on government's proper purpose.
open_items.required_action: In GOV-LES-T1-W02-CORRECTED-WEEK, distinguish the purpose of studying Government from the purpose of government. Attribute the original line to the source; teach political science as a field of study and cite Constitution s.14(2)(b) for Nigeria's constitutional statement. open_items.detail: The sources-of-power list overgeneralises inheritance, conflates constitutional power with elections, and labels expert knowledge as 'position of authority'.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, distinguish constitutional allocation from electoral selection; present inheritance as a possible source in hereditary systems rather than a universal rule; and distinguish positional authority from expertise/technical authority. Attribute the textbook taxonomy.

open_items.detail: The source attributes three types to Max Weber but calls them sources of political authority and abbreviates legal-rational authority to 'legal'.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, accurately attribute Weber's three ideal types of legitimate domination/authority as traditional, charismatic and legal-rational, explain them as ideal types, and cite a dated scholarly source.

open_items.detail: The source names Obas, Emirs and Obis as traditional-authority examples without qualifying the diversity and changing legal roles of traditional rulers in Nigeria.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, describe these as examples of traditional titles, not holders of uniform constitutional powers. Use the 2009 APRM Nigeria report only as historical context; verify any current role against the relevant state's current law.

open_items.detail: The source generalises that political power in Africa is derived from military overthrow. Historical research documents coups in some African countries, but describes uneven distribution and distinct waves; it does not support treating coups as the general or normal source of political power across Africa.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, attribute coups as a historical phenomenon in particular countries and periods, not a continent-wide rule or ordinary route to authority. Use dated sources and explain the constitutional norm against unconstitutional changes. Keep discussion high-level and non-operational.

open_items.detail: The source's military-authority category describes a broad right to maintain law and order. Nigeria's Constitution gives the Armed Forces defined responsibilities and separately establishes the Nigeria Police Force; the military does not have an unlimited general policing mandate.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, distinguish the Nigeria Police Force's duties from the Armed Forces' constitutional functions under ss.214 and 217, including limits and conditions in s.217(2)(c). Keep this civic and high-level, with no operational guidance.

Explain that foreign recognition is a separate external dimension; treat the listed factors as possible influences, not an exhaustive universal test.

open_items.detail: The source gives Jean Bodin's dates as 1530–1596 and attributes a modern theory of sovereignty to him. Scholarly reference dates him 1529/30–1596 and identifies The Six Books of the Commonwealth (1576) as his major sovereignty work.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, use the precise date range 1529/30–1596 (noting 1530 as a common rounded form), identify the 1576 work, and accurately attribute Bodin's historical definition as absolute and perpetual power of a commonwealth. Explain its period context rather than presenting it as current universal law.

open_items.detail: The characteristics section says a sovereign state 'receives order from none' and that its powers cannot be limited. This is a classical doctrinal position, not an uncontested description of modern international law.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, distinguish Bodin's historical doctrine from contemporary international law. Explain sovereign equality and good-faith Charter obligations under UN Charter Article 2(1)–(2); do not teach sovereignty as exemption from all international obligations.

open_items.detail: The source defines de facto sovereignty by acquisition through force and de jure sovereignty by acquisition under domestic law. Modern scholarship distinguishes factual/effective control from normative/legal status; these are not simply two methods of acquisition.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, define de facto in terms of actual control and de jure in terms of legal entitlement/status or recognition; explain that control and legal status may diverge. Also distinguish internal/external dimensions from legal/political perspectives, and avoid defining internal authority as applying only to nationals.

open_items.detail: The source states that democracy is 'the best form of government'. This is a normative evaluation, not an objective settled fact; scholarship records both broad support and continuing disagreement about democracy's justification and institutional forms.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, attribute the claim to proponents or to the source's viewpoint, present major arguments and criticisms neutrally, and distinguish empirical claims about democratic performance from normative arguments about desirability.

open_items.detail: The source's features list uses 'one man, one vote' and emphasizes majority rule without explicitly explaining minority-rights protection and constitutional limits.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, use inclusive 'one person, one vote' language and explain that majority decision-making operates within constitutional rights, rule of law and protections for minorities. Keep this as a normative/institutional explanation, not a claim that every country meets the ideal.

open_items.detail: The source generalises that democracy in an 'illiterate society' is dangerous and that elections produce violence and malpractice. These are not universal facts and the literacy claim risks stigmatizing whole populations.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, present these as attributed criticisms or context-dependent risks, avoid stereotyping people by literacy, and distinguish possible electoral malpractice from the defining features of democracy. Do not reproduce sensational or graphic detail.

open_items.detail: The communalism section presents collective land ownership, absence of private property/classes and barter as universal features. African land-tenure research describes varied and overlapping communal, individual and other rights; the textbook list is an idealized model, not a uniform African or current Nigerian legal order.
open_items.required_action: In GOV-LES-T1-W05-CORRECTED-WEEK, explicitly label communalism as a political/economic model or ideal type. Explain that communal land tenure varies and can coexist with individual rights and other tenure arrangements; do not generalize one model to all communities or present it as current law.

open_items.detail: The source calls feudalism a uniform 'primitive system of government' practised in Western Europe in the Middle Ages and describes kings granting fiefs to subjects. Scholarship treats 'feudalism' as a contested retrospective term with varied meanings and regionally different institutions.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, define the narrow feudo-vassalic use of the term, describe the Western European medieval context without implying uniformity, and explain fiefs and lord-vassal obligations as historically varied arrangements. Attribute the historiographical debate and avoid presenting every vassal as a king's subject.

open_items.detail: The source uses 'serf' and 'vassal' as if they were interchangeable. Historical scholarship distinguishes peasant servile status from the lord-vassal relationship, which often involved members of the landed elite.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, define serf/villein and vassal separately. Explain that serfdom is not simply slavery or ordinary paid service, and that vassalage is not synonymous with serfdom. Cite a dated medieval-history source.

open_items.detail: The source says industrialisation brought about the collapse of feudalism. The decline of serfdom in England is documented from roughly 1300–1500, before the Industrial Revolution, and scholarship identifies multiple economic, demographic, legal and social causes.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, replace the single-cause industrialisation claim with a dated, region-specific account. Distinguish the decline of serfdom from the broader and contested transition from feudal institutions to capitalist economies; do not imply one simultaneous European endpoint.

open_items.detail: The source claims feudalism laid the foundation for capitalism and uniformly created order/security. These are debated historical interpretations, not settled universal benefits.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, attribute these as arguments made by some accounts, explain the context and limits, and avoid a simple inevitable progression from feudalism to capitalism. Cite dated historical scholarship.

open_items.detail: The source presents constant war, insecurity and absence of national government as universal features of feudalism. These varied by period and place and should not be generalized to all medieval Western Europe.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, frame these as criticisms or features documented in particular contexts; distinguish decentralized authority from the claim that no national government existed everywhere. Avoid sensational or graphic detail.

open_items.detail: The source defines socialism mainly as government ownership of production and attributes the formulation of socialism to Karl Marx. Socialist thought and movements predate Marx; the term gained currency in the early nineteenth century among several distinct movements.
open_items.required_action: In GOV-LES-T1-W06-CORRECTED-WEEK, distinguish socialism as a broad family of ideas from state-socialist models. Note that Marx was an influential theorist, not the originator of all socialism; distinguish socialism from social democracy and other mixed-economy arrangements. Attribute features that apply only to particular models.

open_items.detail: The source gives Karl Marx's dates as 1816–1883. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy records 1818–1883.
open_items.required_action: Correct the date to 1818–1883 and cite the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. Do not imply Marx originated all socialist thought; cite pre-Marxian socialist movements.

open_items.detail: The source states that no country has ever practiced communism, while describing communism as state ownership of everything. Scholarship distinguishes historical communist-party states and state-socialist models from the theoretical stateless, classless communist ideal.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, distinguish communist-party governments and historical state-socialist systems from the theoretical classless/stateless ideal. Attribute the source's absolute claim and explain the distinction; do not present state ownership as the full theoretical definition.

open_items.detail: The source says capitalism emerged after the fall of socialism 'in the 1900s', treats minimal government as a defining feature and closely associates capitalism with democracy. Capitalism predates the twentieth century; capitalist economies can be regulated/mixed and can exist under democratic or authoritarian political regimes.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, correct the chronology; distinguish laissez-faire capitalism from regulated/mixed capitalist economies; distinguish economic systems from political regimes; and explain that the late-twentieth-century collapse or transformation of some state-socialist systems did not mean socialism disappeared everywhere. Do not claim capitalism is inherently democratic.

open_items.detail: The class list at lines 510–517 has broken numbering and conflates peasants, wage workers and marginal groups. It also describes the comprador bourgeoisie using a moralized/criminal stereotype rather than its political-economic meaning.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, define bourgeoisie and proletariat by their relationship to ownership and wage labour; distinguish peasants from wage workers; treat lumpenproletariat as a contested historical term, not all unemployed people or a security category; define national and comprador bourgeoisie as analytical categories concerning domestic accumulation and relations with foreign capital. Do not label individuals or groups as criminal based on class terminology. Preserve the original numbering defect in the source record.

open_items.detail: The source says Italian Fascism began in 1922 and ended in 1943. The movement was founded in 1919; Mussolini came to power in 1922 and was deposed in 1943; a German-backed Fascist successor regime continued in northern Italy until 1945.
open_items.required_action: In GOV-LES-T1-W07-CORRECTED-WEEK, distinguish the 1919 movement foundation, 1922 accession to government, Mussolini's 1943 removal and the successor regime's 1943–1945 period. Do not collapse these into one date range.

open_items.detail: The source generalizes that fascism rejects religion and both capitalism and socialism. Italian Fascism's relationship with religion and the economy was more complex; the Lateran Treaties were signed with the Catholic Church in 1929, and private property and business remained under the regime.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, present fascism as a historically varied ideological family. Qualify claims about religion and capitalism using the Italian case; distinguish anti-Marxist/anti-liberal rhetoric from the actual institutions and alliances of the regime. Attribute generalizations rather than stating them as universal facts.

open_items.detail: The 1933–1945 dates for Nazi rule in Germany are accurate. The racial-superiority statement at line 579 is the Nazis' false racist ideology, not a fact about any human group.
open_items.required_action: In GOV-LES-T1-W07-CORRECTED-WEEK, state the 1933–1945 dates, identify racial superiority as a false racist belief promoted by the Nazi regime, and explain that race is not a biological hierarchy. Attribute the ideology and reject its claim; do not reproduce propaganda or graphic detail.

open_items.detail: The source says totalitarianism is also called authoritarianism. Political-science literature distinguishes the concepts: authoritarianism is broader, while totalitarianism is generally used for more ideologically driven regimes seeking pervasive control. The boundary is debated.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, define totalitarianism and authoritarianism separately, explain their relationship and the scholarly debate, and avoid using them as synonyms.

open_items.detail: The source's language about absolute control over every person, idea and property is too literal. Totalitarianism is an analytical concept/ideal type describing an ambition for pervasive ideological and institutional control, not proof of perfect control.
open_items.required_action: In the corrected supplement, describe totalitarian features as regime aims and institutional patterns, not literal omnipotence. Distinguish documented features from analytical generalizations and avoid sensational or graphic examples.
